prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active forms, which led to incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, and I still think it is the strongest case on the table. The chain runs from proglucagon processing and the identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, through Holst's human incretin physiology and Drucker's work on mechanisms of action, to drugs that are now confirmed by large randomized outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The work is original, the interpretation is stable and recognition is timely. In my opening I chose Knudsen as the third name. After reading colleagues I move to Mojsov. Four of five colleagues independently built the trio around the discovery side, and I find the argument persuasive that a Physiology or Medicine citation is best anchored in what GLP-1 is and what it does, with the drug story following from that. Knudsen's engineering of liraglutide and semaglutide is decisive for the drugs but is a development achievement, and the citation can still acknowledge the therapeutic consequence.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Habener is not among the credited names, so a trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov omits a central figure in the early proglucagon and peptide work, and Mojsov's priority for identifying the active peptide is disputed. Dropping Knudsen leaves out the person whose chemistry made the physiology usable by patients. If the Committee judges that the prize should reward the transformation of care as much as the discovery, this configuration is weaker and the one I submitted in my opening would be the better one. If credit cannot be allocated defensibly within three names, the Committee might look at a cleaner alternative such as the unfolded protein response, where two names carry the story.

responses.point: El-Manira ranked GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and put optogenetics second, stressing its causal, cell-type-specific control of circuits, including motor and spinal circuits.
responses.response: I agree on the GLP-1 trio and have moved to it. On optogenetics I am more cautious than you. The impact on circuit neuroscience is not in doubt, but it is a method, and I ranked it fourth. Six credited names for three places also make this the least resolvable allocation on the shortlist. A discovery of the channelrhodopsins (Nagel, Hegemann) plus a neuronal-application part (Deisseroth) would need two prize parts and excludes Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck. I do not think that is a clean, defensible outcome for a first-ranked prize.

responses.point: Perlmann argued that the mechanistic chain from basic physiology to drug is clear and the recognition is arguably overdue, but that Knudsen's industrial development is an alternative or fourth credit rather than part of the core physiology, and flagged Habener's absence.
responses.response: I accept your framing that Knudsen is a different kind of contribution and have changed my trio accordingly. I would still flag your own point about Habener. If we cannot treat the early peptide work fairly with the names supplied, the citation should be worded around the physiology and the active peptides, not around priority for a single finding. We also differ on mTOR. You put Sabatini and Schreiber both in contention with Hall, whereas I see Hall as the clear anchor and the second and third names as unresolved, which is why it stays at the bottom of my list.

responses.point: Sandberg also ranked GLP-1 first, but chose Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, with Knudsen representing translation into liraglutide and semaglutide, and called Mojsov's early peptide work real but contested.
responses.response: This was my own opening view and I take it seriously. The disagreement is whether the prize should end at the discovery or include the drug engineer. I now think the discovery framing is the more defensible one. Mojsov's contribution is contested, but so is any choice among four names, and excluding Knudsen is easier to justify as a prize-scope decision than excluding a discoverer is as a credit decision. If you can show that the physiology could not have become a drug without the specific half-life engineering, I would hear that, but I do not think it changes the nature of the discovery.

responses.point: Svenningsson, our chair, put imatinib and BCR-ABL second, calling it original, clear and transformative, and arguably overdue, while noting the underlying chemistry and earlier oncogene work are outside the credited names.
responses.response: I agree that the clinical impact of imatinib is exceptional and the follow-up is long, but I did not place it in my top eight, and the reasons are your own caveats. Druker, Lydon and Sawyers describe a drug development and clinical proof achievement, and the discoveries on which it rests (the Philadelphia chromosome and the BCR-ABL fusion, and the chemistry that made the compound) are outside the credited list. I think that makes the allocation harder than for the unfolded protein response, which also would not need to be split across a development pipeline. I would like to hear why you rank it above both B006 and B047.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked anti-TNF therapy for rheumatoid arthritis second, with Feldmann and Maini as a natural pair, calling it a bench-to-bedside discovery of lasting impact whose recognition is long awaited.
responses.response: The anti-TNF story has a clear conceptual claim, since showing that a single cytokine drives the inflammatory cascade in the synovium and that blocking it works established a therapeutic principle. I did not rank it. My concern is the one you raise, that those who cloned TNF and the engineers of the antibodies are not among the credited names, so a Feldmann-Maini prize would honour the clinical translation alone. That is not disqualifying, and I would be interested in how you weigh it against the UPR, where the mechanism is cleaner but the clinical consequence is indirect. Only two of us placed it in the top eight, so I suspect it will not gather four votes.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should be the third GLP-1 laureate, and whether the absence of Habener from the credited names makes a fair allocation impossible.
Whether the Committee prefers to reward the discovery of GLP-1 physiology or the creation of long-acting drugs.
Whether CAR-T (B047) is mature enough, given Eshhar's absence from the credited names and the unresolved solid-tumour and long-term toxicity questions.
Whether the unfolded protein response, with a clean pair of names but indirect clinical impact, should be preferred over translational candidates if GLP-1 allocation stalls.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented co-authors (including Castelo-Branco, Betsholtz, Ernfors, Frisen, Lundeberg, Kharchenko and Sandberg) are not credited names on any shortlisted ballot, and the spatial transcriptomics paper I co-authored is not a shortlisted topic. I share an institution with colleagues on the committee, which I do not treat as a conflict.
